scenes.tts: One protein has two jobs. Which job did the cell miss when losing it slowed division? Chapter one's rule can help: a result chooses only where the twins disagree. Its last test put the protein back, and division recovered.
scenes.visual: Open on the carried world from chapter 1: the TEAL and ORANGE twin cells side by side, each about 65% of frame height, both stalled mid-division. A purple protein blob in each cell has two small glowing tags beside it, one labelled 'job 1', one labelled 'job 2'. Across the top, show the question 'Which job did the cell miss?' from the first frame. On 'Chapter one's rule', the wide bottom bar appears under the twins, reading 'SAME / DIFFERENT' in its resting state. On 'put the protein back', a purple strand labelled 'resistant copy' enters each cell, purple blobs return and both cells finish dividing. The job tags attach to the returned blobs without appearing to split from them.
scenes.caption: One protein has two jobs. Which job did the cell miss when losing it slowed division? Chapter one's rule can help: a result chooses only where the twins disagree. Its last test put the protein back, and division recovered.
scenes.narration: One protein has two jobs. Which job did the cell miss when losing it slowed division? Chapter one's rule can help: a result chooses only where the twins disagree. Its last test put the protein back, and division recovered.

scenes.visual: Title 'Two Jobs, One Protein' fades in across the top for 2 seconds while the job tags keep orbiting the purple blobs.

scenes.tts: The protein is clathrin. One protein can do more than one task in a cell. Clathrin's best-known job is endocytosis. Clathrin coats small pockets of the cell's surface membrane, which pinch inward and carry material into the cell.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the top edge of the teal cell so a stretch of membrane fills the lower two thirds of the frame. Purple clathrin blobs gather on the inner face of the membrane in a small cluster; the membrane under them dents inward, deepens into a pocket, and pinches off as a small purple-coated vesicle carrying a few white dots inward. This repeats slowly at two or three spots along the membrane. The label 'endocytosis' appears only after the first pocket has pinched off. A small corner tag reads 'schematic'.
scenes.caption: The protein is clathrin. One protein can do more than one task in a cell. Clathrin's best-known job is endocytosis. Clathrin coats small pockets of the cell's surface membrane, which pinch inward and carry material into the cell.
scenes.narration: The protein is clathrin. One protein can do more than one task in a cell. Clathrin's best-known job is endocytosis. Clathrin coats small pockets of the cell's surface membrane, which pinch inward and carry material into the cell.

scenes.tts: In two thousand and five, Stephen Royle and colleagues silenced clathrin in human cells in a dish. Mitosis, the division of one cell into two, took longer. So clathrin matters for division. But how?
scenes.caption: In 2005, Stephen Royle and colleagues silenced clathrin in human cells in a dish. Mitosis, the division of one cell into two, took longer. So clathrin matters for division. But how?
scenes.visual: Pull back to one large cell, centre frame. The white hairpin from chapter 1 (the R N A interference) pairs with the purple strand, the strand breaks, and the purple blobs fade away. The cell rounds up and begins to divide; beside it a horizontal timer bar labelled 'time in mitosis' grows. A faint dashed mark on the bar shows 'control'; the bar grows past it and keeps going, and only then does the cell finish splitting in two. Corner label: 'Royle, Bright and Lagnado, 2005'; the timer bar is tagged 'schematic'. On 'But how?', a white question mark settles over the two daughter cells.
scenes.narration: In 2005, Stephen Royle and colleagues silenced clathrin in human cells in a dish. Mitosis, the division of one cell into two, took longer. So clathrin matters for division. But how?

scenes.tts: Here are the twins again. In the teal twin, clathrin works in mitosis itself. In the orange twin, it helps only through endocytosis, and division suffers indirectly. Interference works over a few days, so an indirect route would have time to build.
scenes.visual: The cell splits back into the TEAL and ORANGE twins in their usual places, both dividing slowly. Teal twin: purple blobs settle directly along the white fibres of a simple two-pole spindle, and a short arrow runs from the spindle-bound blobs to a label 'mitosis'. Orange twin: purple blobs sit only at the membrane making inward pockets as in the previous scene, and a longer arrow runs from 'endocytosis' around the cell to 'mitosis', drawn as two linked steps. On 'over a few days', a small day counter under both twins ticks 1, 2, 3 while the orange arrow's middle link thickens.
scenes.caption: Here are the twins again. In the teal twin, clathrin works in mitosis itself. In the orange twin, it helps only through endocytosis, and division suffers indirectly. Interference works over a few days, so an indirect route would have time to build.
scenes.narration: Here are the twins again. In the teal twin, clathrin works in mitosis itself. In the orange twin, it helps only through endocytosis, and division suffers indirectly. Interference works over a few days, so an indirect route would have time to build.

scenes.tts: Now the rescue from chapter one. Silence clathrin in both twins, then put back the whole protein, in a form the interference cannot touch. If mitosis returns to normal, does that choose between the twins?
scenes.visual: In both twins the white hairpin breaks the purple strand and the 'time in mitosis' bar under each cell grows long. Then a purple strand labelled 'full-length, resistant' drifts into both cells; the hairpin bumps against it and slides off, and purple blobs return. The question card appears at the top: 'Does rescue choose?' Both cells keep dividing slowly.
scenes.caption: Now the rescue from chapter one. Silence clathrin in both twins, then put back the whole protein, in a form the interference cannot touch. If mitosis returns to normal, does that choose between the twins?
scenes.narration: Now the rescue from chapter one. Silence clathrin in both twins, then put back the whole protein, in a form the interference cannot touch. If mitosis returns to normal, does that choose between the twins?

scenes.visual: Hold both twins, the returned purple blobs and the question card. The only motion is both cells slowly dividing and the purple blobs drifting.

scenes.tts: It cannot. The whole protein brings back both jobs, so both twins predict rescue. And in the experiment, full-length clathrin did rescue mitosis. That strongly ties the defect to clathrin loss. Which job, rescue cannot say.
scenes.visual: In both twins the two job tags reappear on every purple blob, both lit. The 'time in mitosis' bar under each cell shrinks back to the dashed 'control' mark at the same moment. The bottom bar fills grey and reads 'SAME: both rescue'. On 'did rescue mitosis', a small tick and the corner label 'Royle and colleagues, 2005' appear. On the last sentence, a white question mark returns between the two job tags.
scenes.caption: It cannot. The whole protein brings back both jobs, so both twins predict rescue. And in the experiment, full-length clathrin did rescue mitosis. That strongly ties the defect to clathrin loss. Which job, rescue cannot say.
scenes.narration: It cannot. The whole protein brings back both jobs, so both twins predict rescue. And in the experiment, full-length clathrin did rescue mitosis. That strongly ties the defect to clathrin loss. Which job, rescue cannot say.

scenes.tts: They also put back only the front part of clathrin. It did not rescue. But a failed rescue is hard to read. The piece might be made at the wrong level, fold badly, or sit in the wrong place.
scenes.visual: One large cell, centre. A shorter purple strand labelled 'front part only' drifts in and makes small, half-sized purple blobs. The 'time in mitosis' bar stays long, past the dashed control mark. On 'hard to read', three small white check boxes appear beside the cell, each unticked, labelled 'amount', 'folded', 'place'. The cell keeps dividing slowly.
scenes.caption: They also put back only the front part of clathrin. It did not rescue. But a failed rescue is hard to read. The piece might be made at the wrong level, fold badly, or sit in the wrong place.
scenes.narration: They also put back only the front part of clathrin. It did not rescue. But a failed rescue is hard to read. The piece might be made at the wrong level, fold badly, or sit in the wrong place.

scenes.tts: To make the twins disagree, change the protein itself. Build a resistant copy that keeps one job and loses the other. This is a separation-of-function mutant. First show that one job still works and the other does not. Then check its amount, folding and location.
scenes.visual: Back to the TEAL and ORANGE twins. In both cells a purple strand labelled 'one job only' drifts in; its purple blobs carry only one lit tag, 'job 1', with the 'job 2' tag drawn as a dim, broken outline. A shared check panel between the twins first confirms 'job 1 works' and 'job 2 lost', then adds one compact line: 'amount · folding · location'. The bottom bar's pointer moves from grey 'SAME' toward GOLD 'DIFFERENT' and stops there, glowing, while the twins' mitotic outcomes remain hidden.
scenes.caption: To make the twins disagree, change the protein itself. Build a resistant copy that keeps one job and loses the other. This is a separation-of-function mutant. First show that one job still works and the other does not. Then check its amount, folding and location.
scenes.narration: To make the twins disagree, change the protein itself. Build a resistant copy that keeps one job and loses the other. This is a separation-of-function mutant. First show that one job still works and the other does not. Then check its amount, folding and location.

scenes.tts: Royle and Leon Lagnado built such a copy the next year. What does each twin predict for it? That is a question for you in the text below. Work it out before you read on.
scenes.visual: A small corner label reads 'Royle and Lagnado, 2006'. Both twins hold the 'one job only' copy, but their timer bars and mitotic outcomes remain hidden. A question card at the top reads 'What does each twin predict?' and a small downward arrow under it points off the bottom of the frame, toward the page below. Only the cells' outlines and protein blobs drift gently; nothing is resolved on screen.
scenes.caption: Royle and Leon Lagnado built such a copy the next year. What does each twin predict for it? That is a question for you in the text below. Work it out before you read on.
scenes.narration: Royle and Leon Lagnado built such a copy the next year. What does each twin predict for it? That is a question for you in the text below. Work it out before you read on.

scenes.tts: So rescue answers one question: did losing the protein cause the defect? To ask which job, use a copy that keeps one and loses the other. Before you test it, write down what each twin predicts. Rescue supports the protein's role; split its jobs to learn which.
scenes.visual: Two small panels fly in across the middle, each a shrunken version of its own scene: the full-length rescue with its grey 'SAME' bar, and the 'one job only' copy with its GOLD 'DIFFERENT' bar. On 'cause the defect?', the first panel brightens; on 'which job', the second brightens and the first dims. On 'write down', a small blank card appears under each twin. On the last sentence the teal and orange twins glow once behind the panels.
